clinicalPearls: Progressive enlargement, thickening and lobulation of the nose from sebaceous gland hyperplasia and fibrosis, representing the phymatous form of rosacea
It predominantly affects the lower nose, producing a bulbous, irregular contour with dilated follicular openings
It occurs far more often in men and usually develops in the context of long-standing rosacea
Contrary to popular belief, it is not caused by alcohol excess
A rare but important concern is squamous or basal cell carcinoma arising within or mimicking rhinophyma
Advanced disease is managed surgically or with ablative techniques to recontour the nose
reference.pathophysiology: Rhinophyma is the end stage of phymatous rosacea, in which chronic inflammation drives marked hyperplasia of sebaceous glands, dermal fibrosis and connective-tissue overgrowth of the nasal skin. Progressive sebaceous and fibrous expansion distorts the nasal contour and enlarges follicular openings. The underlying rosacea-associated vascular and inflammatory changes, rather than any dietary or alcohol factor, account for the disfigurement, and occasionally cutaneous malignancy develops within the thickened tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Other phymas of rosacea (for example of the chin or ears)
Basal or squamous cell carcinoma of the nose
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the characteristic appearance and rosacea history
Biopsy of any suspicious nodule or ulcer to exclude carcinoma
Assessment of the extent and functional impact including nasal airway
redFlags: A non-healing ulcer, bleeding nodule or rapidly growing lesion suggesting malignancy
Features suggesting granulomatous or lymphomatous infiltration
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but progressive if untreated and can be cosmetically and functionally disabling; surgical recontouring generally gives good results, though rosacea persists.
pitfalls: Attributing the condition to alcohol and stigmatising the patient
Missing a carcinoma arising within rhinophymatous tissue
Neglecting treatment of the underlying rosacea
